findings.finding_to_cite: Title: 'MedCite: Can Language Models Generate Verifiable Text for Medicine?' The eight authors are Xiao Wang, Mengjue Tan, Qiao Jin, Guangzhi Xiong, Yu Hu, Aidong Zhang, Zhiyong Lu and Minjia Zhang. Findings of ACL 2025, pp. 18891-18913. The setup is Llama-3-8B-Instruct on BioASQ-Y/N, with MedCPT top-3 citations against PubMed (Table 2). Non-RAG generation reaches 71.36 EM, with citation recall 59.05 and precision 52.93. Adding RAG raises accuracy to 82.85 EM, but citation recall falls to 49.01 and precision to 42.77. The authors explain that the citation metrics check whether a statement is supported, not whether it is correct, so citations can still support a hallucinated statement that is irrelevant to the question. They conclude that text and citation quality must be assessed together, and they make answer correctness a prerequisite for citation evaluation. A secondary finding (Table 7): medicine-specialised NLI attribution judges agree poorly with physicians, with Cohen's kappa 0.18-0.26 on the recall judge and at most 0.22 on the precision judge.
findings.positioning_sentence: In medical QA, adding retrieval raised answer accuracy from 71.4 to 82.9 EM while citation recall fell from 59.1 to 49.0, because a supported citation need not attach to a correct statement \cite{wang2025medcite}.

findings.source_checked: arXiv API + abs page for 2412.18004 (v1 only) + full arXiv PDF text (Sec. 5, Fig. 3); Crossref /works/10.1145/3731120.3744592 for the published ICTIR 2025 version (also indexed as DBLP conf/ictir/WallatHRA25 via Semantic Scholar)
findings.finding_to_cite: The work is published at ICTIR 2025 (ACM SIGIR), pp. 22-32, doi 10.1145/3731120.3744592, under a retitled name: 'Correctness is not Faithfulness in Retrieval Augmented Generation Attributions'. The arXiv title is '...in RAG Attributions'. Authors: Jonas Wallat, Maria Heuss, Maarten de Rijke, Avishek Anand. The paper separates two properties. Citation correctness asks whether the cited document supports the statement. Citation faithfulness asks whether the model actually relied on that document. They name the failure mode 'post-rationalization': the model forms an answer from parametric memory, then looks for a supporting document. Setup: Command-R+ on NaturalQuestions, BM25 + ColBERTv2, top-5 documents. They appended a previously cited short statement to other documents. The model then cited the forged document in three conditions: 12% (116/936) for random documents, 57% for relevant-but-uncited documents, and 55% for documents cited for another reason. The abstract summarises this as attributed answers lacking faithfulness in up to 57% of citations. All figures are from arXiv v1. The ACM camera-ready could not be read.
findings.positioning_sentence: A citation can be correct without being faithful: a retrieval-tuned model cited documents into which a previously cited statement had been inserted in up to 57% of cases, which indicates post-rationalisation rather than a record of what was used \cite{wallat2025correctness}.

findings.finding_to_cite: ALCE (Gao, Yen, Yu, Chen; EMNLP 2023, pp. 6465-6488) reports three cases where correctness and citation quality move apart. (1) CLOSEDBOOK+POSTCITE 'delivers strong correctness but poor citation quality'. Answering without retrieval beats VANILLA on correctness on ELI5 and QAMPARI and trails it by only about 2 points on ASQA (38.3 vs 40.4 EM recall). Its post-hoc citation recall on ASQA is 26.7 vs 73.6, which is 47 points lower. On ELI5, claim recall is 18.6 vs 12.0, yet citation recall is 15.5 vs 51.1. The authors attribute this to closed-book text being correct but not similar to any retrieved passage, so citations are hard to match afterwards. (2) Summarising or snippeting passages improves correctness, but on ASQA and ELI5 this 'comes at a cost of citation quality due to the lossy compression'. On ASQA, SUMM moves EM recall from 40.4 to 43.3 while citation recall falls from 73.6 to 68.9 and precision from 72.5 to 61.8. (3) GPT-4 brings consistent but limited correctness gains, 'often at a cost of citation quality'.
findings.positioning_sentence: On ASQA, answering closed-book and citing post hoc keeps correctness within two points of retrieval-grounded generation while citation recall falls from 73.6 to 26.7, and compressing retrieved passages raises correctness at a cost in citation quality \cite{gao2023alce}.

findings.finding_to_cite: Paper: 'Attribute or Abstain: Large Language Models as Long Document Assistants', Jan Buchmann, Xiao Liu, Iryna Gurevych, EMNLP 2024, pp. 8113-8140. The study tests evidence quality as an abstention gate. Attributability scored by TRUE or MiniCheck orders responses for selective prediction, and response-quality/coverage AUC is compared against a random ordering. Evidence quality predicts response quality on single-fact datasets: Natural Questions, Evidence Inference, ContractNLI, and to some extent WiCE. On multi-fact QASPER and GovReport the gain over random is small. The reason given is that models answer correctly but fail to point to all the necessary evidence. The abstract states that evidence quality can predict response quality on simple responses, 'but not so for complex responses'. They also note that earlier work was inconclusive: reranking by evidence quality improved responses in Bohnet et al. (2022) but not in Gao et al. (2023).
findings.positioning_sentence: Used as an abstention signal, evidence quality predicts response quality on single-fact tasks but not on multi-fact ones, where models answer correctly yet fail to cite all the evidence, so a support-keyed gate can withhold correct answers \cite{buchmann2024attribute}.
